ruleIntents.intent: Checks that every rendered (non-hidden) image element on the page resolves to EITHER a non-empty accessible name OR an explicitly decorative role (presentation/none). It is a pure presence/absence-of-name check on the accessibility tree: it does NOT judge whether the alt text is correct, meaningful, or equivalent to the image content — only that some non-empty name string exists, or the image is legitimately marked decorative. "Empty" is defined post-trim, so whitespace-only alt counts as empty. The decorative escape hatch is gated by Presentational Roles Conflict Resolution (e.g. role=none on a focusable element does NOT count as decorative).
ruleIntents.scLimb: SC 1.1.1's core "Non-text Content has a text alternative" requirement, but ONLY the first two of the SC's exception limbs: (a) content that "serves the same purpose / conveys information" must HAVE a text alternative (here proxied as: name string is non-empty), and (b) "Decoration, Formatting, Invisible" content "is implemented in a way that it can be ignored by assistive technology" (here proxied as: role=presentation/none or empty alt). It exercises the MARKUP/name-existence facet only. It does NOT touch the SC's other limbs — Controls/Input (1.1.1 functional name), Time-Based Media, Test, Sensory, or CAPTCHA — and it deliberately does NOT assess text-alternative QUALITY/equivalence (G94/G95 adequacy), which the SC actually requires.
ruleIntents.applicability: Applies to HTML img elements and any element with a semantic role of img (e.g. div role="img"), EXCEPT elements that are programmatically hidden. "Programmatically hidden" removes aria-hidden=true, display:none, and visibility:hidden subtrees from scope (these become Inapplicable, not Pass/Fail). Off-screen positioning (margin-left:-9999px) does NOT remove applicability — off-screen images are still in scope.
ruleIntents.expectation: Each in-scope target element either (1) has a computed accessible name that is not the empty string "" (after the accessible-name computation, which trims surrounding whitespace), OR (2) has a semantic role of none or presentation. Name can come from alt, aria-label, aria-labelledby (referenced element may itself be display:none and still supply the name), or title. PASS if either condition holds; FAIL if the element is exposed as a semantic img with an empty name.

syntheticNarrowness: Every page is a single isolated img on an otherwise blank body — no surrounding text, links, captions or layout context, so the rule never has to disambiguate an image that is functionally decorative-in-context vs informative-in-context (the SC's hardest judgment).

All informative images use the SAME placeholder alt string 'W3C logo' that genuinely describes the asset, so the test set NEVER exercises the SC's actual requirement that the alternative be EQUIVALENT/adequate: a wrong, generic ('image'), filename-derived ('w3c-logo.png'), or misleading alt would all PASS this rule yet fail real 1.1.1. Quality is entirely out of scope by construction.

Decorative-vs-informative is asserted by markup fiat (the author pre-declares alt="" / role=presentation), never tested against whether the image actually IS decorative. A meaningful image suppressed with alt="" (an F38-style real failure) would PASS here.

Only single, static, raster / role=img div / one trivial SVG. No functional images (links/buttons wrapping an img, input type=image, area in image-map), no CSS background images conveying content, no /

Name-source coverage is one-attribute-at-a-time and never tested for precedence conflicts (e.g. alt vs aria-label vs aria-labelledby disagreeing), nor for broken aria-labelledby (dangling/typo idref), nor multi-token labelledby concatenation.

Hidden-handling is reduced to three textbook CSS/ARIA mechanisms (aria-hidden, display:none, visibility:hidden) on a directly-wrapped image; no offscreen clip(), opacity:0, hidden attribute, inert, collapsed-zero-size, or conditionally toggled/JS-revealed images that change applicability dynamically.

Edge cases are minimal-token tricks (one literal space in alt; one tabindex on role=none) rather than realistic content; the whitespace case only tests a single ASCII space, not tabs/newlines/NBSP/zero-width or all-punctuation 'alt' that AT effectively ignores.

No internationalization, no very long alt, no duplicated adjacent images, and no real photographic/document screenshots — so a vision-capable judge gets no signal that would distinguish a correct alt from a plausible-but-wrong one, which is exactly where this rule's pass-but-still-fails-SC gap lives.

ruleIntents.intent: Checks that any element the author "marked as decorative" actually stays out of the way of assistive technology — i.e., it is either NOT in the accessibility tree or carries a computed semantic role of none/presentation. The rule's real job is catching the Presentational Roles Conflict Resolution failure: an element flagged decorative (role=none/presentation, or img alt="") that ALSO carries something forcing it back into the tree (a global aria-* property like aria-label/aria-labelledby, or being focusable), so its presentational role is overridden by its implicit role and it leaks to AT. It is a pure DOM/CSS/accessibility-tree structural check — it does NOT evaluate whether the image content is genuinely decorative vs. meaningful, nor whether any alternative text is correct.
ruleIntents.scLimb: The "marked as decorative / pure-decoration" limb of SC 1.1.1: per WCAG, "if non-text content is pure decoration... it is implemented in a way that it can be ignored by assistive technology." This rule polices only that exception clause — that author-declared-decorative non-text content is in fact ignorable by AT — NOT the dominant limb requiring a meaningful text alternative for informative non-text content. It is mapped as a SECONDARY requirement: the rule itself is broader (it fires on text/non-decorative elements too, e.g. nav), and only the subset where the target is decorative NON-TEXT content constitutes an actual 1.1.1 failure.
ruleIntents.applicability: Applies to any element that is "marked as decorative," defined as: (a) it has an explicit role of none or presentation; OR (b) it is an img element with alt="" (empty string) and no explicit role. Authoring intent only — not whether the element is actually pure decoration. Note: for the 1.1.1 mapping specifically, only decorative NON-TEXT content counts as an SC failure; the rule's own applicability is wider.
ruleIntents.expectation: Each target element must EITHER (1) not be included in the accessibility tree (e.g. via aria-hidden=true, hidden / display:none, visibility:hidden), OR (2) have a computed semantic role of none or presentation. It FAILS when the decorative element is (or would be, absent programmatic hiding) included in the tree with its implicit role due to the presentational-roles conflict-resolution trigger — i.e. it defines a global ARIA attribute (aria-label, aria-labelledby, etc.) or is focusable. Per-element own attributes (e.g. alt on an img with role=presentation) do NOT trigger the conflict, so they pass.

Only img, svg, and nav element types appear; no role=presentation on tables/lists (where conflict resolution and required-owned-element semantics behave specially), buttons, links, or other interactive controls.

Synthetic content uses the same w3c-logo.png and trivial yellow-circle SVG throughout; the rule never sees ambiguous content where a human/AT user would disagree about whether exposure causes a real barrier, nor screen-reader-actual behavior differences the rule's own Accessibility Support note warns about.

No cantTell / partial-automation scenarios and no aria-hidden-on-focusable edge case (the glossary calls out that focusable + aria-hidden is treated as NOT in the tree, but a browser may still expose it) — a known real-world ambiguity left entirely untested.

ruleIntents.intent: Checks that every `<input type="image">` (an image-as-submit-button) that is exposed in the accessibility tree has a non-empty accessible name, AND that the name is not the browser-default placeholder "Submit Query" (the localized default the ANC falls back to when no real label source exists). It is a pure accessible-name-presence test computed via the input type=image Accessible Name Computation: it walks alt -> aria-label -> aria-labelledby -> title and fails if the resolved name is empty or equals the default. It does NOT judge whether a present name is meaningful/descriptive (a non-empty "Search" passes; the rule never asks if that name correctly describes the icon's function).
ruleIntents.scLimb: SC 1.1.1 limb: non-text content that is a "Control" / functional non-text content — the image button conveys function, so its text alternative must "serve the equivalent purpose" (the controls/input branch of 1.1.1, supported by technique H36 "alt on images used as submit buttons", G94/G95). It does NOT exercise the decorative/CSS-image, CAPTCHA, sensory, or test/time-based-media limbs. Note the rule dual-maps: 1.1.1 covers it being non-text content needing an alt; 4.1.2 covers it being a UI component needing a name. The rule conflates both into one accessible-name check.

ruleIntents.intent: Checks that an SVG image element which the author has explicitly marked as meaningful (via an explicit ARIA role of img, graphics-document, or graphics-symbol) and which is exposed to assistive technology actually carries a non-empty accessible name. It is purely a name-presence check on graphics: does the computed accessible name string have content, or is it empty (""). It does NOT judge name quality/accuracy, nor does it cover decorative SVGs or SVGs lacking an explicit role.
ruleIntents.scLimb: SC 1.1.1's core requirement that non-text content presenting information has a text alternative serving an equivalent purpose. Specifically the "informative image" limb (the General/img case), not the decorative/CAPTCHA/sensory/control/test exceptions. It enforces only the existence of the text alternative for an author-declared-meaningful graphic; it does not test equivalence of purpose.
ruleIntents.applicability: Applies to any SVG element (the root <svg> or an inner SVG shape like <circle>) that has an EXPLICIT semantic role of exactly one of img, graphics-document, or graphics-symbol, AND is included in the accessibility tree. Excluded: SVGs with no explicit role (even though <svg> implicitly maps to graphics-document — the rule deliberately ignores implicit roles due to inconsistent browser/SVG-AAM support), SVGs removed from the tree (aria-hidden=true, etc.), and SVGs with any other explicit role (e.g. graphics-object). Input aspects are DOM tree + CSS styling.
ruleIntents.expectation: Each in-scope target element has a computed accessible name that is not the empty string. The accessible name may come from aria-label, aria-labelledby, or a non-empty SVG <title> child. An empty <title></title> fails, and notably an SVG <text> element (rendered visible text inside the graphic) does NOT contribute to the accessible name, so a graphic that visually shows "1 circle" via <text> still fails. No requirement on name correctness, length, or whether it matches the visual content.

ruleIntents.intent: Checks that every <object> element which embeds non-text media (image, audio, or video MIME type) and is exposed in the accessibility tree has a non-empty accessible name. It is purely a name-presence check on object elements: it computes the object's accessible name (from title, aria-label, or aria-labelledby) and fails if that name resolves to the empty string "". It does NOT judge whether the name is meaningful/descriptive, and it does NOT look at any other non-text content mechanism (img alt, etc.) — only the object element and only the accessible-name-empty-vs-nonempty distinction.
ruleIntents.scLimb: 1.1.1 Non-text Content, the core "all non-text content ... has a text alternative that serves the equivalent purpose" requirement — specifically the existence/presence of a programmatically-determinable text alternative (accessible name) for embedded non-text media rendered via <object>. It targets the general non-text-content case (image/audio/video that conveys content), not the named exceptions (controls, CAPTCHA, decoration, time-based media as its own SC). It enforces only the "has a text alternative at all" half of 1.1.1, leaving the "serves the equivalent purpose" half explicitly out of scope (per Background).
ruleIntents.applicability: Applies to an <object> element where ALL of: (a) it is included in the accessibility tree (so display:none, visibility:hidden, aria-hidden=true, and role=presentation/none remove it); (b) it has no explicit role (any author-set role, e.g. role="img", makes it inapplicable — handled by other rules); and (c) it embeds a resource whose MIME type is image, audio, or video. Objects embedding HTML/other MIME types, objects whose resource fails to load (so fallback content renders instead), and non-object elements are all inapplicable.

ruleIntents.intent: The rule checks one narrow, syntactic fact: that every HTML element which is an "inheriting semantic link" exposed in the accessibility tree has a computed accessible name that is not the empty string "". It does NOT evaluate whether that name is meaningful, descriptive, or conveys the link's purpose — only non-emptiness. The accessible name can come from any standard source (link text/child content, alt on a contained img, aria-label, aria-labelledby, title on the a or on the contained img). A link whose only content is an image fails when that image is decorative/unnamed (alt="", role="presentation"/"none", title="", empty/broken aria-labelledby, or no alt at all), because the link is then left with no name. Crucially for SC 1.1.1, the rule is really an accessible-name presence check on link elements; 1.1.1 enters only obliquely via the special case where the link is an HTML area element (an image map region), which is simultaneously a link AND non-text content.
ruleIntents.scLimb: For SC 1.1.1, the rule exercises the "text alternative that serves the equivalent purpose" limb only insofar as a link's accessible name is supplied by non-text content. Concretely it touches 1.1.1 via the area element of an image map (Passed Example 10 area alt="Sun" vs Failed Example 9 area with no alt): the area IS non-text content acting as a control, and its alt provides the text alternative. More broadly it touches the F89 limb — "image that is the only content of a link must have a text alternative" — but it tests this as accessible-name presence, not as 1.1.1 conformance. The rule's own mapping is explicit that 1.1.1 is a SECONDARY/related requirement, not the one it was designed to test (it was designed for 4.1.2 / 2.4.4 / 2.4.9), and that "Most failed examples satisfy this success criterion."
ruleIntents.applicability: Applies to any HTML element that is an inheriting semantic link AND is included in the accessibility tree. "Inheriting semantic link" covers: a/area elements with an href, elements with explicit role="link", and elements with a role inheriting from link such as role="doc-biblioref". Excluded by applicability: elements whose link role has been overridden (a with role="button" -> Inapplicable Ex1), a/area with no href so no link role (Inapplicable Ex5/Ex6), and anything removed from the accessibility tree via display:none, visibility:hidden, or aria-hidden="true" (Inapplicable Ex2-4). Note Failed Ex10 shows role="none" on a focusable a does NOT remove applicability, because Presentational Roles Conflict Resolution restores the link role.
ruleIntents.expectation: Each in-scope (target) link element has an accessible name that is not the empty string "". Pass = non-empty accessible name from any source (content text, img alt, aria-label, aria-labelledby pointing at non-empty text, title on the link or on a contained img). Fail = accessible name computes to "" (e.g. empty a, link wrapping only a decorative/unnamed image, empty title, aria-labelledby to empty or missing id). There is NO descriptiveness/adequacy check — a non-empty but useless name like "click here" would still pass this rule.

No dynamic/JS-populated names (name injected after load, name set via JS, lazy-loaded images) — all names are static at parse time, unlike real SPAs.
Image-loading state is irrelevant here because names come from attributes, but real 1.1.1 also cares about broken-image fallback / failed src, which is untested.
No internationalization: all names are English; no RTL, no non-Latin alt text, no implications of language on the accessible-name computation.

The decorative-image failures are clean textbook cases (single img, explicit alt=""/role=presentation); real pages mix a decorative icon with adjacent text, or have the icon as a separate sibling link, which this corpus never shows.
Only HTML-native and a couple ARIA link patterns appear; no framework/component-library link patterns, no <Link> components, no nested interactive content edge cases.

ruleIntents.intent: Checks the converse of "missing alt text": it finds visible images (img/svg/canvas) that ARE hidden from assistive technology and verifies that hiding them was justified — i.e. that each such image is genuinely PURELY DECORATIVE and not conveying information. The rule does not check whether informative images have a name; it checks whether images deliberately given NO name (alt="", aria-hidden, role=none/presentation, or an unnamed svg/canvas) are actually decorative. The pass/fail hinges on a semantic judgment of the image's visual content (fireworks = decorative; W3C logo = informative), which is impossible to decide from markup alone — the two representative cases are byte-for-byte structurally identical (alt="" on an img) and differ ONLY in the pixels and adjacent text.
ruleIntents.scLimb: The "pure decoration" carve-out of SC 1.1.1: the clause stating that non-text content that is "pure decoration, is used only for visual formatting, or is not presented to users" is exempt and "can be implemented in a way that it can be ignored by assistive technology." This rule polices the boundary of that exemption — confirming that content claiming the decoration exemption (and thus hidden from AT) qualifies for it. It does NOT exercise the main limb (informative non-text content must have a text alternative serving an equivalent purpose); that is the inverse rule (e.g. 23a2a8 / non-empty-alt rules).
ruleIntents.applicability: Applies to any visible img, canvas, or svg element that is ignored by assistive technologies via one of three mechanisms: (a) excluded from the accessibility tree (e.g. alt="", aria-hidden=true, role=none/presentation), (b) an svg with empty accessible name AND semantic role graphics-document, or (c) a canvas with empty accessible name AND no explicit semantic role. Hard exceptions: never applies if the element has a flat-tree ancestor that is "named from author" (e.g. an img inside a button/link that supplies the name via aria-label — the parent's name covers it), or if it is an img whose image-request state is not "completely available" (broken/loading images). Also excludes elements that are not visible (display:none, off-screen, transparent canvas) and elements that ARE in the a11y tree with a non-empty name (those are someone else's rule).
ruleIntents.expectation: Each in-scope (AT-ignored) element must be PURELY DECORATIVE — it must convey no information that is unavailable elsewhere on the page. If the hidden image actually carries information (a logo, a meaningful icon, text rendered on a canvas), the rule FAILS because information has been silently dropped for AT users. Outcome mapping: any failed outcome means SC 1.1.1 is not satisfied; all-passed or inapplicable means the SC still needs further testing (the rule is non-conclusive for passing). Note: an informative image marked decorative can still meet WCAG conformance via a conforming alternative version if equivalent text is adjacent — but it still fails THIS rule.

Real markup combines and conflicts them (aria-hidden on a focusable link, alt text plus role=presentation, CSS visibility toggles, JS that hides/shows) and uses spacer GIFs, tracking pixels, and 1x1 images not represented here

Whole categories of decorative non-text content that 1.1.1 covers are explicitly OUT of this rule's scope and thus untested by it: CSS background-images (punted to another rule), ::before/::after content images, generated content, icon fonts, and inline data-URI/sprite images

No internationalization, RTL, dynamic, or stateful scenarios (carousels, lazy-loaded images, images that become informative on hover/focus); fixtures are static English snippets with hard-coded local test assets

ruleIntents.intent: Whether an image's accessible name is SEMANTICALLY CORRECT — i.e., it actually describes/serves the same purpose as the pixels the image shows — not merely whether a name is present and non-empty. The element already has a non-empty accessible name (that's the applicability gate); the rule judges the truthfulness/adequacy of that name against the real image content. Concretely: alt="W3C logo" on the W3C logo passes; alt="ERCIM logo" on the same W3C logo fails because the name names the wrong thing. This is the human-judgment half of 1.1.1 that presence-checkers (does alt exist?) cannot do, hence the not-fully-automatable flag — deciding equivalence requires actually perceiving the image and comparing meaning.
ruleIntents.scLimb: SC 1.1.1 limb: the core "text alternatives ... serve the equivalent purpose" requirement for informative/meaningful non-text content (the G94/G95 path; F30 is the named failure for non-equivalent alternatives like wrong/placeholder text). It does NOT exercise the decorative ("pure decoration / can be ignored" → empty alt), CAPTCHA, sensory, or controls/input limbs of 1.1.1 — those are explicitly pushed to Inapplicable (empty name, role=presentation) or out of scope. It is purely the "name exists AND must be an accurate equivalent" sub-limb.
ruleIntents.applicability: Any img, canvas, or svg element that is (a) visible and (b) has a NON-EMPTY accessible name. Excluded: elements with an ancestor in the flat tree that is "named from author" (e.g., an svg inside a link/button whose own aria-label supplies the name — Inapplicable Example 8); and img elements whose current request state is not "completely available" (broken/loading images — Inapplicable Example 9). Also implicitly out of scope by the visibility/non-empty-name gate: display:none images, role=presentation/empty-alt decorative images, aria-hidden images, transparent canvases, and CSS background images (which the rule explicitly says must be tested separately). So the rule deliberately narrows to exactly the case "a perceivable image that claims a name."
ruleIntents.expectation: Each in-scope target's accessible name must serve an equivalent purpose to the non-text content of that target — the name must accurately convey what the image is/communicates. PASS = name is an accurate equivalent (alt="W3C logo" on the W3C logo; svg aria-label="HTML 5 logo" on the HTML5 logo; canvas aria-label="W3C logo" rendering the W3C logo). FAIL = name is present but inaccurate/mismatched (alt="ERCIM logo" on the W3C logo; svg aria-label="W3C" on the HTML5 logo; canvas aria-label="HTML 5 logo" rendering the W3C logo). Note the asymmetric outcome mapping: any FAIL ⇒ SC not satisfied, but all PASS ⇒ "needs further testing" (the rule alone can't confirm full 1.1.1 conformance).

syntheticNarrowness: Only TWO images in the entire corpus (the W3C logo and the HTML5 logo, plus an unused fireworks/pdf-icon for decorative cases) — every PASS/FAIL hinges on recognizing one of two famous tech logos; real-world 1.1.1 covers photos, charts, diagrams, screenshots, infographics, maps, icons, equations, and unfamiliar content where 'equivalent purpose' is far more subjective.

All FAIL cases are 'names a clearly DIFFERENT well-known entity' (W3C logo labeled 'ERCIM'/'W3C' vs HTML5) — a crisp, near-binary mismatch. Real failures are usually subtler: vague but not-wrong names ('image', 'logo', 'graphic'), partially-correct-but-incomplete names that drop information, redundant names duplicating adjacent text, or filename/placeholder leakage (F30) — none of which appear.

The accessible name is always supplied by a single, simplest mechanism per element type (img→alt, svg→aria-label+role=img, canvas→aria-label). No accname computation complexity: no aria-labelledby chains, no title attribute, no figure/figcaption, no concatenation of multiple sources, no whitespace/ordering edge cases.

Each page contains exactly ONE element with no surrounding context, content, or competing landmarks. Real 1.1.1 judgment depends heavily on context — whether the image is a link target, conveys data redundant with nearby text, or is the sole carrier of information — which a one-element page cannot represent.

Logos are images of TEXT, so 'descriptive' is trivially the brand name; this sidesteps the genuinely hard 1.1.1 question of how much/what detail a text alternative for a complex or pictorial image must include (G94 'equivalent purpose' vs G95 'brief description' tension is never actually tested).
All names are short noun phrases in English; no long descriptions, no multilingual content (despite Language being a listed input aspect), no cases where brevity vs completeness must be weighed.

Image content is static and immediately available; the canvas cases rely on JS having drawn the image, but no animation, no state-dependent imagery, no responsive/art-directed variants, and the only 'state' nuance (broken image) is shunted to Inapplicable rather than tested as a content-vs-name scenario.

FAIL outcomes require an oracle that already KNOWS the image is the W3C/HTML5 logo; the corpus never includes a hard case where a name is plausibly-but-arguably wrong, so it tests crisp recognition rather than the borderline equivalence judgments that make this SC not-fully-automatable in practice.

aspects.title: Information conveyed exclusively by a CSS background-image (no img element, no DOM text equivalent)
aspects.description: An element carries meaning purely through a CSS background-image — set in a stylesheet rule, an inline style= attribute, or injected by script — and that same meaning exists nowhere as real text in the DOM. Because there is no img/svg/object/input element and no alt slot, every ACT 1.1.1 rule (which is scoped to elements that can hold an accessible name) returns Inapplicable; there is no target to evaluate. A human must look at the rendered page, recognize that a background image is carrying information (a price banner, a status/stock icon, a 'SOLD OUT' stamp, a required-field marker, a weather condition glyph, a logo), and then verify whether that exact information is ALSO available as text elsewhere on the page. This is a two-step semantic + visual judgment: (1) does this background image depict required information, and (2) is that information redundant in the DOM text?
aspects.scLimb: The core 'all non-text content that conveys information has a text alternative' requirement (G94 / 'serves the same purpose'), applied to the background-image mechanism that the SC covers but the ACT accessible-name rules structurally cannot reach.
aspects.whyUncovered: Every ACT 1.1.1 rule targets elements that can hold an accessible name (img, role=img, svg[role], object, input[type=image], a). A CSS background image is none of these, so all rules return Inapplicable and the corpus has zero background-image pages. Automated checkers cannot do this either: they cannot reliably enumerate which background images carry information vs decoration, and even if they could, deciding whether the info is 'already conveyed elsewhere on the page' is a meaning-comparison task between a rendered image and surrounding prose. Trusted Tester gives this its own dedicated manual test (7.C) precisely because it is not automatable.

references.quote: it is not possible to associate text alternatives with images that are included via CSS. Text alternatives are necessary for people who cannot see images that convey information that is required to understand the content of the page.

This failure would apply equally in a case where the background image was declared in the HTML style attribute, as well as in a case where the background image declaration was created dynamically in a client script
Test 7.C — `1.1.1-decorative-background-image` Test Condition: The background image is not the only means used to convey important information.

aspects.constructionStrategy: Single self-contained HTML page. Put the load-bearing fact ONLY inside a CSS background-image (stylesheet rule, inline style=, or a JS-set class), referencing a real raster/SVG asset whose pixels show the fact. Keep the visible DOM text deliberately silent on that fact so hiding the background loses it. Vary the carrier (stylesheet vs inline style vs script-injected) and the info type (price, stock status, required marker, badge, weather condition) so the set exercises the F3 declaration variants. To make a PASS control, add one page where the same background image's info IS duplicated in adjacent text.
suggestedScenarios: Pricing card whose only rate '19.3% APR Typical Variable' lives inside a stylesheet background-image PNG; visible text says only 'Where else would you find a better interest rate?' (verbatim F3 example).
Book list <ul> where each <li> stock status (New / Limited / In stock / Out of stock) is shown ONLY by a CSS-class background-image icon; the <li> text is just the title (second F3 example).
Login form whose 'required field' asterisks are background images on <label> spans, with no '*' or 'required' text anywhere in the markup.
Product hero where the only 'SALE 50% OFF' badge is an inline style='background:url(sale.png)' on an empty <div>, and no text mentions the sale.
Weather widget showing today's condition solely as a script-injected background-image (sun/cloud/rain) on a <span>; the temperature is text but the condition is image-only.
Government form marking the single 'mandatory' section by a red-icon background image on its <div>, with no textual 'mandatory' label.
PASS control: a status badge background-image whose meaning ('In stock') is also written as visible text immediately beside it.

aspects.title: A genuinely informative/functional image marked decorative (alt="" / role=presentation) so AT cannot reach it
aspects.description: An image that actually conveys needed information or function is declared decorative — alt="", role=presentation, or role=none — so it is correctly hidden from AT per the markup and the ACT name-presence/decorative rules all PASS (the markup is internally consistent). The real failure is that the image SHOULD have carried a text alternative: it is the sole carrier of a fact or function (a 'Verified seller' badge, a size chart, a signature image, the only diagram of a recipe step, a wizard progress meter, a severe-weather pictogram). Detecting this requires viewing the rendered image, judging that it carries information the user needs, and concluding the author's 'decorative' declaration is wrong. It is the exact inverse of the corpus's tested case (correctly-decorative) and is a pure intent/meaning judgment that no syntactic check can make.
aspects.scLimb: The boundary between the SC's 'conveys information ⇒ must have a text alternative' limb and its 'Decoration/Formatting/Invisible ⇒ ignored by AT' exception limb — specifically catching mis-classification where author fiat wrongly invokes the decorative exception (F38/F39 applied contextually).
aspects.whyUncovered: The synthetic corpus asserts decorative-vs-informative by MARKUP FIAT — the author pre-declares alt=""/role=presentation and the rule trusts it; the rule can never fail a 'decorative' image because it never asks whether the image is truly decorative. So a meaningful image with alt="" PASSES 23a2a8/46ca7f/e88epe by construction. Automated tools share this blind spot: an empty alt is syntactically valid, and no tool can know that THIS particular badge is the only verification signal or that THIS empty-alt image is the only copy of the diagram. Trusted Tester 7.B requires the human to first decide 'is the image the only means of conveying important information?'

references.quote: When an image is used for decoration, spacing or other purpose that is not part of the meaningful content in the page then the image has no meaning and should be ignored
Determine if the image is the only means of conveying important information on the page.

Sometimes there is non-text content that really is not meant to be seen or understood by the user. Transparent images used to move text over on a page; an invisible image that is used to track usage statistics; and a swirl in the corner that conveys no information but just fills up a blank space

aspects.constructionStrategy: Single self-contained page. Render a real image whose pixels carry a needed fact or function, then suppress it from AT via alt="", role=presentation, or role=none. Ensure NO redundant text equivalent exists so the fact is genuinely lost to AT. Vary the suppression mechanism and the lost-info type (badge, measurement table, signature, instructional diagram, progress, alert). Include a borderline PASS control: a truly decorative swirl/spacer correctly marked alt="" beside meaningful text, so judges must distinguish real decoration from mis-marked information.
suggestedScenarios: 'Verified seller' green-check badge next to a listing as — the only verification signal, hidden from AT.
E-commerce size chart shown only as , so screen-reader users get no measurements at all.
Bank statement where the account holder's handwritten signature image is alt='' even though it is the proof-of-identity being shown.
Recipe step illustrated by a single fold-the-dough diagram that is the only instruction, with no textual equivalent.
'Page 3 of 4' wizard progress meter rendered as an image with role='none', removing the user's only sense of position.
Weather-alert banner whose 'severe storm' pictogram is the only indicator and is marked alt='' (text says only 'Weather update').
PASS control: a purely aesthetic corner swirl correctly marked alt='' adjacent to a paragraph that holds all the meaning.

aspects.title: Non-empty alt that is not actually an alternative: filename, placeholder, or auto-generated label (F30)
aspects.description: An image has a non-empty accessible name that LOOKS like content but is not a usable substitute for the image: a filename ('DSC_0481.jpg', 'hero-2.png', 'banner_final_v3'), a CMS auto-caption ('image', 'photo', 'picture'), a programming reference ('img_001', 'Intro#2'), or an upload artifact ('Screenshot 2024-03-11 at 14.22.png'). Because the string is non-empty, every ACT presence rule PASSES. The descriptive-name rule (qt1vmo) only catches this if the placeholder happens to name a DIFFERENT identifiable asset; a filename like 'IMG_4823.jpg' on a sunset photo names nothing identifiable, so qt1vmo cannot judge it wrong against the asset. A human recognizes 'this is a filename / generic placeholder, not a description' — a meaning/intent judgment about the STRING itself relative to what the image depicts.
aspects.scLimb: The core 'text alternative that serves the equivalent purpose' requirement — the equivalence/adequacy facet (G94 'serves the same purpose'), which the ACT presence rules deliberately do not assess and which qt1vmo only covers for identity mismatch.
aspects.whyUncovered: The corpus never uses filename-style or placeholder alt values; all informative pages use the genuinely-descriptive string 'W3C logo', so presence always passes and quality is out of scope by construction. qt1vmo's failures are IDENTITY mismatches (wrong logo named), not NON-ALTERNATIVE strings. A purely automated keyword blocklist ('image','photo','spacer') is brittle and the SC explicitly does not mandate one; deciding that 'sunset_beach_final.jpg' is a filename-not-alt, or that 'Banner' is too generic, requires reading the string AS a human and comparing it to what the image actually shows. F30 is defined as a manual 'is this actually a text alternative?' check.

aspects.constructionStrategy: Single self-contained page with one or more informative images. Give each a non-empty alt that is a real non-alternative: a camera/CMS filename, a versioned export name, a generic placeholder ('image'/'photo'), or a programming reference ('prod-9921-thumb-2'). The image's pixels must depict something specific so a human can see the string conveys none of it. Avoid making the placeholder coincidentally name a different identifiable brand asset (that would be the already-covered qt1vmo identity case). Add a PASS control where the alt genuinely describes the depicted content.
suggestedScenarios: News article hero photo of a protest with alt='DSC_0481.JPG' — non-empty, passes presence, conveys nothing.
Product gallery where each thumbnail's alt is its CMS slug, e.g. alt='prod-9921-thumb-2'.
Staff directory where every distinct headshot has alt='photo' regardless of who is pictured.
Infographic embedded with alt='infographic_final_v3.png' — a versioned filename masquerading as a description.
Three different charts on one page all carrying the export default alt='Chart.jpg'.
Tutorial screenshot with alt='Screenshot 2024-03-11 at 14.22.png' on an image showing specific UI steps.
PASS control: the same protest photo with alt describing the depicted scene ('Crowd marching past city hall with banners').

aspects.title: Alt literally describes the image but is wrong for the image's purpose-in-context (link target or control function)
aspects.description: An image has an alt that correctly identifies the depicted thing — so it passes presence rules and even passes qt1vmo (it IS descriptive of the image in isolation) — but it is the WRONG alternative for the role the image plays on this page. The Understanding doc makes this explicit: the SAME globe image needs alt 'International Travel' on a travel site but 'International Campuses' on a university site; a newspaper-front-page thumbnail that links to a homepage needs the publication name, not a description of the masthead photo. The same applies to images used AS controls: a printer icon button needs 'Print this page' not 'inkjet printer'; a magnifying-glass submit button needs 'Search' not 'magnifying glass'; an image-map area / input type=image needs its destination/action. Judging equivalence requires understanding the image's FUNCTION and context (what it links to, what action it performs, what point it illustrates), not just what it literally depicts.
aspects.scLimb: Two intertwined limbs the corpus never exercises: (a) the core 'serves the SAME PURPOSE' equivalence requirement evaluated in CONTEXT (G94), and (b) the SC's distinct 'non-text content that is a control or accepts user input ⇒ name describes its PURPOSE' limb (functional images: links, buttons, input type=image, image-map areas).
aspects.whyUncovered: qt1vmo evaluates whether the name describes the IMAGE in isolation — every corpus page is one isolated img on a blank body with no link, no control, no surrounding prose — so it has no notion of the image's purpose-in-context. A literal-but-context-wrong alt ('globe') passes even when the globe is a link whose purpose is 'International Travel'. The functional/control limb is entirely absent from the corpus (no a/img, button/img, input[type=image], or area). Automated tools cannot infer an image's intended communicative purpose from page context or link destination; this is the SC's hardest judgment.

references.quote: An image of the world that is used on a travel site as a link to the International Travel section has the text alternative "International Travel". The same image is used as a link on a university website with the text alternative "International Campuses".
A thumbnail image of the front page of a newspaper links to the home page of the "Smallville Times". The text alternative says "Smallville Times".

For non-text content that is a control or accepts user input, such as images used as submit buttons, image maps or complex animations, a name is provided to describe the purpose of the non-text content

aspects.constructionStrategy: Single self-contained page. Wrap an informative image in a real link or control (a href, button, input type=image, or area in an image map) and give it an alt that literally and correctly names the DEPICTION but omits the link destination / action purpose. The image's pixels must look right for the depiction so the failure is purely contextual, not an identity mismatch. Vary between link-purpose cases (globe→travel, thumbnail→publication) and control-purpose cases (printer→Print, magnifier→Search, image-map area→room). Include a PASS control where the alt names the purpose ('Print this page').
suggestedScenarios: Globe wrapped in with alt='globe' — literally correct, but the link purpose 'International Travel' is lost.
Newspaper-front-page thumbnail linking to a publisher homepage with alt='Newspaper with election headline' (describes the photo) instead of the publication name.
Printer-icon <button> with alt='inkjet printer' on a control whose purpose is 'Print this page'.
Magnifying-glass <input type='image'> submit button with alt='magnifying glass' instead of 'Search'.
Image-map building floor plan where each <area> alt describes the room's appearance rather than 'Go to Room 101 information'.
Red-octagon image used as a 'Cancel order' button with alt='red octagon' rather than its function.
PASS control: the same printer-icon button with alt='Print this page'.

aspects.title: Complex image (chart/diagram/map) has a plausible alt/long description that drops information the image conveys (F67)
aspects.description: An informative complex image — a data chart, a diagram, a map, a schematic — has a non-empty, descriptive-sounding short alt and/or a long description, so it PASSES every presence rule and passes qt1vmo (the name correctly identifies the image in general). But the short alt is insufficient for a complex image, and/or the long description omits specific information the image actually conveys: a venue map whose description names the venues but gives no locations/addresses; a chart whose description gives totals but not the trend; a flow diagram whose prose lists boxes but not the connections. The SC requires the alternative to present the SAME information (G94 short + G73/G74 long descriptions). Catching this requires viewing the image, enumerating the information it conveys, and confirming each datum is or is not present in the text — a same-purpose/completeness comparison that is the inverse of a presence check.
aspects.scLimb: The core 'text alternative that serves the equivalent purpose / presents the same information' requirement applied to complex non-text content (charts/diagrams/maps) needing long descriptions — the adequacy/completeness facet the ACT presence rules explicitly disclaim and that the corpus never builds (no complex images at all).
aspects.whyUncovered: The corpus contains only single static raster /role=img divs and one trivial SVG — no charts, diagrams, maps, or any complex image needing a long description. The presence rules only check that some non-empty name exists; qt1vmo checks gross identity, not partial-equivalence, so an alt can correctly identify a chart yet drop its trend or specific data and qt1vmo PASSES it. Automated tools cannot read what a chart depicts nor verify a prose description against it. F67 is explicitly a manual 'does the long description serve the same purpose / present the same information?' check.

references.quote: the failure that occurs when the long description for non-text content does not serve the same purpose or does not present the same information as the non-text content

While this description provides useful information, it does not convey the same information as the image because it provides no specific location information such as the address or the distance of each location from some fixed point.

The longer description identifies the type of chart, provides a high-level summary of the data, trends and implications comparable to those available from the chart. Where possible and practical, the actual data is provided in a table.

aspects.constructionStrategy: Single self-contained page rendering a real complex image (a bar/line chart, a labeled diagram, or a map — can be an inline SVG or a raster) whose pixels encode multiple data points/relationships. Provide a short alt plus a long description (in a figcaption, adjacent prose, or aria-describedby) that is plausible but verifiably DROPS specific information the image shows (omits the trend, the addresses, the connections, the outlier). The deficit must be discoverable only by reading the image against the text. Add a PASS control whose long description (or data table) fully reconstructs the image's information.
suggestedScenarios: Olympic-venue street map with a long description naming the venues but giving no addresses or distances (verbatim F67 example).
Bar chart whose alt/figcaption gives the four totals but never states the year-over-year trend or which value is the outlier the chart highlights.
Flowchart diagram whose prose lists every box but omits the decision branches/arrows connecting them.
Subway/transit map image whose description names the lines but not which stations connect to which.
Org chart screenshot described as 'company org chart' with reporting lines (who reports to whom) absent from the text.
Scatter plot with alt 'Height vs weight scatter plot' that omits the visible correlation and the cluster of outliers.
PASS control: the same bar chart accompanied by a data table that reproduces every value plus a sentence stating the trend.

aspects.title: Image of meaningful text whose alt does not reproduce the same text
aspects.description: An image whose primary content IS text — a logo wordmark, a quote rendered as a graphic, a pull-quote image, a 'terms' graphic, a scanned notice, a price/coupon banner that is essentially words — has a non-empty alt that describes or summarizes the image instead of reproducing the words. Because the alt is non-empty it passes presence rules, and because it may correctly identify the image ('promotional banner') it can pass qt1vmo, yet a screen-reader user never receives the actual text the image displays. For an image of meaningful text the alternative must contain the SAME text. Distinguishing this requires reading the words in the image and confirming they appear in the alt — a transcription-equivalence judgment a checker cannot perform (it cannot OCR reliably, and the corpus has no text-in-image cases).
aspects.scLimb: The core 'serves the equivalent purpose' requirement for the specific case of images of text — Trusted Tester 7.A step 1.d: the accessible name must contain the SAME text the image displays. (Note: this is the 1.1.1 text-alternative facet, distinct from 1.4.5 Images of Text.)
aspects.whyUncovered: The corpus's informative images are logos described as 'W3C logo' — a label, never a case where the alt must REPRODUCE displayed words. Presence rules only require a non-empty name; qt1vmo checks whether the name identifies the image, not whether it transcribes text the image shows. No fully-automated checker reliably OCRs an image and compares the extracted text to the alt, and the SC does not mandate one. Trusted Tester carves out a specific manual step (7.A.1.d) for 'image of meaningful text', confirming it is a separate human judgment.

references.quote: If the image is of **meaningful text**, ANDI Output must contain the **same text**.

If the text in the "text alternative" cannot be used in place of the non-text content without losing information or function then it fails because it is not, in fact, an alternative to the non-text content.

Text alternatives are a primary way for making information accessible because they can be rendered through any sensory modality (for example, visual, auditory or tactile) to match the needs of the user.

aspects.constructionStrategy: Single self-contained page rendering a real image whose pixels are predominantly words (a quote graphic, coupon code banner, scanned notice, or wordmark with a tagline). Give it a non-empty alt that summarizes or labels the image ('promotional banner', 'inspirational quote') rather than reproducing the displayed words, so the actual text is lost to AT. The words in the image must be specific and load-bearing (a coupon code, a quote, a deadline). Add a PASS control where the alt contains the verbatim text shown in the image.
suggestedScenarios: Coupon banner image showing 'Use code SAVE20 at checkout' with alt='promotional banner' — the code is never spoken.
Pull-quote rendered as a graphic ('The only thing we have to fear is fear itself') with alt='inspirational quote image' rather than the quote text.
Scanned office-closure notice image with alt='notice' instead of the dates and instructions it displays.
Pricing graphic where the plan tiers and prices are baked into the image, with alt='pricing options'.
Logo lockup whose tagline ('Banking made simple') is part of the image, with alt='company logo' that drops the tagline.
Event flyer image with date/time/venue as text-in-image and alt='event flyer'.
PASS control: the coupon banner with alt reproducing the displayed text including 'SAVE20'.

aspects.title: Text look-alike (homoglyph / Unicode confusable) glyphs representing text with no text alternative (F71)
aspects.description: Visible 'text' on the page is actually composed of characters from another script chosen because their glyphs LOOK like the intended letters/digits — Cyrillic 'о' for Latin 'o', Greek 'ϲ' for 'c', Cyrillic letter for '3'. Sighted users read the intended word; a screen reader reads garbled output or silence because the codepoints are not the letters they resemble. Per F71 this is effectively non-text content (the meaning rides on glyph shapes, not the actual characters) and it lacks the required text alternative. No img/svg/object element is involved, so all ACT 1.1.1 rules are Inapplicable. Catching it requires comparing the rendered glyphs against the actual codepoints / what a screen reader would announce in the page's language — a human reading judgment.
aspects.scLimb: The SC's 'all non-text content ... has a text alternative' requirement extended (per F71) to text-look-alike glyph substitution, where displayed meaning is carried by glyph shape rather than the encoded characters and no text alternative is provided.
aspects.whyUncovered: The corpus contains only img/role=img/SVG targets; there are no homoglyph/confusable text pages, and every ACT 1.1.1 rule is Inapplicable here because there is no name-bearing element. Reliable automated detection is brittle — confusables span thousands of codepoints across scripts, legitimate multilingual content mixes scripts, and the SC does not mandate a blocklist — so deciding that 'ϲоοk' is Latin 'cook' rendered in confusables (vs legitimate Greek/Cyrillic text) is a human reading-against-language judgment.

references.quote: The objective of this failure condition is to avoid substituting characters whose glyphs look similar to the intended character, for that intended character.

The following word looks, in browsers with appropriate font support, like the English word "cook", yet is composed of the string U+03f2 U+043E U+03BF U+006B, only one of which is a letter from the Western alphabet. This word will not be processed meaningfully, and a text alternative is not provided.
If look-alike glyphs are used, and there is not a text alternative for any range of text that uses look-alike glyphs, then the content does not meet the Success Criterion.

aspects.constructionStrategy: Single self-contained page (lang='en') with visible 'words' built from Unicode confusables so they render as intended English words but encode foreign-script codepoints, with NO text alternative (aria-label / visually-hidden real text) provided. Mix raw confusable characters and the character-entity form (F71 covers both). Make the substituted word load-bearing (a brand name, a heading, a CTA). Add a PASS control using the same visible word in correct Latin characters, and optionally a true-negative of legitimate multilingual content so judges must distinguish abuse from valid script mixing.
suggestedScenarios: Heading that visually reads 'cook' built from U+03F2 U+043E U+03BF U+006B (verbatim F71 example), no text alternative.
A brand wordmark in body text (e.g. 'PayPal') where the 'a' and 'P' are Cyrillic look-alikes, with no real-text label.
A 'Buy Now' CTA link whose visible text uses Cyrillic 'у'/'о' so the screen reader announces garbage.
Same confusable word implemented via numeric character entities (ϲоοk) to exercise F71's entity variant.
A price '$300' where the '3' and '0' are Cyrillic/other-script digit look-alikes, with no aria-label.
A navigation menu mixing legitimate Latin items with one confusable-substituted item, with no text alternative on the substituted one.
PASS control: the same visible word(s) using correct Latin codepoints (and/or a confusable word given a visually-hidden real-text alternative).

pages.scenario: Building-society loan card whose headline rate '19.3% APR Typical Variable' lives only as pixels in a stylesheet background-image SVG; the visible DOM prose says only 'Where else would you find a better interest rate?' (verbatim F3 example 1).
pages.mechanism: The load-bearing price (19.3% APR Typical Variable) is rendered exclusively by `p#bestinterest { background-image: url(svg) }`. A CSS background image generates no accessibility-tree node and cannot carry a text alternative, so a screen-reader user hears the unanswered question and never learns the rate; forced-colors/hide-backgrounds drops it for sighted users too.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: There is no img/svg/role=img/object/input[type=image] — nothing nameable — so every ACT 1.1.1 rule is Inapplicable and axe/WAVE/Lighthouse have no target. They cannot OCR the data-URI SVG to find '19.3% APR', cannot classify the flag as informative vs decorative, and cannot perform the meaning-comparison of whether the rate appears as text elsewhere.

pages.scenario: Record-shop catalogue table where each row's stock status (In stock / Last copy / Pre-order / Sold out) is shown ONLY by a CSS-class background-image glyph in a text-empty leading cell; row text is just artist/title/format/price (F3 example 2 mechanism).
pages.mechanism: Stock status lives only in `td.stock.in/.last/.pre/.sold` background-image glyphs on empty, unlabelled cells, contributing nothing to the accessibility tree. A screen-reader user hears the Sold-out row identically to the In-stock row and could try to buy an unavailable record; hide-backgrounds/forced-colors removes all glyphs.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The status carriers are <td> cells with a CSS background and no nameable element, so ACT 1.1.1 rules are Inapplicable and axe/WAVE/Lighthouse see only empty cells. They cannot OCR the four distinct glyphs, cannot tell they encode mutually exclusive inventory states, and cannot verify 'Sold out' appears nowhere as text.

pages.scenario: Volunteer sign-up form whose required-field markers are red-asterisk background images on empty <span> elements set via the HTML style= attribute, with no '*' character, no 'required' text, and no required/aria-required attribute anywhere (F3 style-attribute carrier).
pages.mechanism: Each `label .mark` is an empty span whose inline-style background-image asterisk is the only 'required' indicator; the span is empty in the accessibility tree and there is no required/aria-required state. A screen-reader user hears 'First name, edit text' with no hint it is mandatory and cannot distinguish required from optional fields.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Every field has a proper <label for>, so no missing-label/missing-alt fires; because no required/aria-required is present, 'required not indicated programmatically' rules also do not trigger (nothing is technically missing). The marker is a background image on a <span>, so ACT 1.1.1 is Inapplicable. Only a human seeing the rendered asterisks can tell mandatory-ness is image-only.

pages.scenario: Restaurant menu where each dish's spice level (1/2/3 chillis) is shown only by chili-pepper background images that JavaScript injects onto empty <span class=heat> from a data-heat attribute; the menu text never says mild/medium/hot (F3 example 3 script-injected carrier).
pages.mechanism: A client script sets `span.heat { background-image }` (one chili tile repeated N times, width=N*16px) from data-heat; the count is a background image on an empty span and never enters the accessibility tree, and data-heat is not exposed as content. A screen-reader user cannot tell the 3-chili Phaal from the 1-chili Daal — a safety-relevant gap.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The glyphs are script-set background images on empty spans — no image-alt target, no accessibility node — so ACT 1.1.1 is Inapplicable. A scanner sees only empty spans (or an inline style url() it cannot interpret), cannot OCR the chili tiles, cannot infer the count encodes intensity, and cannot judge the heat level is missing from text.

pages.scenario: Airline seat-map where exit-row seats (row 12) are flagged only by a green emergency-exit background-image glyph on seat buttons whose accessible names are just the seat numbers; a generic legend mentions exit rows but is not programmatically tied to specific seats.
pages.mechanism: `button.seat.exit` has accessible name = seat number ('12A'); the exit-row status is carried only by the `.exit` background-image glyph, which adds no accessibility node. A screen-reader user hears '12A, button' identically to a normal row, missing the legal/evacuation/cost consequences of an exit-row seat. The unlinked legend cannot be mapped to specific seats by AT.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Every seat button has a non-empty accessible name, so button-name/accessible-name rules pass; the exit indicator is a background image (no image-alt target, no extra node), so the F3 carrier is not a nameable element and ACT 1.1.1 is Inapplicable. Tools cannot OCR the exit glyph, cannot tell exit-row status is missing from the name, nor detect that the legend fails to associate with seats.
